title: Harbour voices: two passages
paragraphs: PASSAGE A — A map made of sound

Before a new pedestrian bridge is built at Pelangi Harbour, a youth research team is creating a public sound map of the waterfront. At twelve fixed locations, members record two minutes of surrounding sound at the same three times each day. They also note the weather and measure sound levels, but they do not record private conversations. Project leader Hana Idris says the aim is to document how the harbour is used, not to declare every loud sound harmful.

The first week showed why consistent methods matter. A festival band occupied the main square on Tuesday, and heavy rain emptied the eastern pier on Thursday. The team kept those recordings but labelled them as unusual and repeated both sessions the following week. Its early map suggests that engine noise is strongest beside the ferry ramps, while bird calls become easier to hear after the final ferry leaves. Shopkeepers have added notes explaining when deliveries, prayer times and fishing auctions usually alter the soundscape.

The town council is considering whether the map could inform a quieter loading schedule near homes. The researchers welcome that interest, but their online display calls every pattern provisional. It cannot show what caused each sound or predict how the bridge will change the area. Idris describes the map as 'a record that helps us ask better questions, not a verdict on the harbour'.
PASSAGE B — The bell at dusk

When I was younger, the ferry bell interrupted the best part of every afternoon. Its two flat notes meant that Grandfather would look up from the watch he was repairing, cover the tiny gears with a cloth and ask me to carry the signboard inside. I blamed the bell for ending our stories. Only years later, while helping him close the shop for the final time, did I notice how many other people moved with it: tea sellers stacked their cups, cyclists turned towards the jetty and a fisherman untied his smallest boat.

I tried to capture the bell on my phone. The recording was clear, yet when I played it indoors, it sounded thinner, separated from the shutters, footsteps and evening wind that had answered it. Grandfather laughed at my disappointment. 'You saved the note,' he said, 'but you expected to save the whole hour.' Now the bell still marks an ending, although I no longer hear it as a thief. It reminds me that a familiar place is made not from one perfect sound, but from people listening and responding to one another.
